articles.description:
I built Check My Ring Size, a free tool where you hold a ring up to your screen and match it to a circle. It sounds like a weekend project. The hard part is one sentence: a web page has no way to ask how big a millimeter is.
If a circle is drawn 104 pixels wide, nothing in the browser tells you whether that is 17 mm on someone's phone or 30 mm on an old monitor. A ring that is 17.3 mm across (a US size 7) has to be drawn at exactly the right size, or the whole tool is worthless. This post is about how I solved that, and the bug that made my first version wrong by a factor of two to three.
Why CSS units don't help
CSS has mm and in, so it is tempting to write width: 17.3mm and move on. Don't. By definition, a CSS inch is 96 CSS pixels, and that is a reference value, not a measurement of you…

articles.author: Neeraj Singhi
articles.description:
The Problem With Implicit Deadline Inheritance


Every production Go service eventually accumulates a category of goroutine leak that evades standard leak detectors: goroutines that are neither blocked nor idle, but consuming real resources while executing work whose results will never be observed. The usual culprit is not a missing defer cancel(). It is a structural mismatch between how context.Context deadlines propagate across goroutine boundaries and how the calling code reasons about cancellation.
This article covers the mechanics of that mismatch, the race conditions it generates, and a propagation ownership model that prevents the failure mode at the design level.
When you derive a child context with context.WithDeadline or context.WithTimeout, the Go runtime registers a cancellatio…
articles.title: Context Propagation Across Goroutine Boundaries: Deadline Inheritance, Cancellation Races, and the Silent Leak

articles.author: TMGS Việt Nam
articles.description:
WatchTowr observed probing of two GeoServer vulnerabilities that appeared aimed at finding vulnerable servers. However, it had not reported successful remote code execution by attackers. Organizations operating GeoServer need to distinguish Internet exposure, vulnerable software and evidence of compromise when assessing their systems.
Eye Security identified Internet-accessible servers, but that finding does not establish how many are vulnerable or compromised. TMGS emphasizes that asset inventory, vulnerability remediation and incident investigation each require their own evidence.
According to SecurityWeek, the two vulnerabilities being probed belong to a chain of five flaws discovered by Rapid7 researcher Jonah Burgess. Combined with other flaws, they can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. This does not establish that either vulnerability independently allows an attacker to take over a server.
GeoServer has released patches. TMGS recommends upgrading to 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7. The absence of reported successful code execution is not a reason to delay remediation while probing is already being observed.
TMGS recommends inventorying GeoServer deployments, recording their actual versions and Internet accessibility, and assigning someone to verify each upgrade. Prioritize Internet-accessible systems and restrict access according to business needs while updates are pending.
For outsourced deployments, TMGS recommends obtaining the post-update version and functional test results from the responsible provider. Completion should include a confirmed version and a working service after the update.
TMGS also recommends reviewing logs and unusual activity, documenting the limits of available evidence and assessing suspicious findings separately. Patching addresses vulnerabilities; conclusions about compromise require investigation evidence.
Read the full analysis on TMGS: https://tmgs.vn/tin-tuc/geoserver-va-khoang-cach-tu-do-quet-den-xam-nhap-i.2fd1ab87-f3af-46c4-a590-00e6d01a6f6e
articles.title: GeoServer probing: distinguishing exposure from confirmed compromise

articles.author: FolioSpan
articles.description:
I built a Telegram alert relay that never sees portfolio data


FolioSpan is a local-first portfolio tracker. When users asked for Telegram delivery of price alerts, the obvious design — send the portfolio to a server, evaluate there, forward the alert — was off the table. The app's whole point is that holdings never leave the device unless you opt in.
So the relay is deliberately blind.
Alert evaluation happens on-device. The app periodically checks prices in the background and composes the finished notification text locally — "Portfolio value crossed 1.00", "BTC moved -6.2% in 24h".
The worker is a dumb pipe. A Cloudflare Worker exposes /link, /webhook, /send, /status. Its KV stores only an opaque link token mapped to a chat ID. No holdings, no prices, no portfolio — ever.
Linking is one-shot. The app opens a t.me/bot?start=<token> URL; the token is single-use with a 10-minute TTL. /stop in Telegram wipes the binding from KV, and the app clears its local credentials on the next status check.
The message travels verbatim. The client posts the finished text to /send; the worker relays it to Telegram HTML-escaped, capped at 3,500 chars and 60 messages/day.
If the relay is compromised tomorrow, the attacker gets a table of random tokens and chat IDs — not a single holding. The privacy contract isn't "we promise not to look"; it's that there is nothing to look at.
No two-way bot. /stop is the only command; anything else gets a help message. Query commands like /portfolio would require the server to see holdings — a different product, not a toggle.
Local-time semantics. Quiet hours and the daily fire cap are enforced by the on-device policy engine before a message is ever produced — the relay doesn't need to know about them.
The full feature note is on the blog: https://getfoliospan.com/blog/price-alerts-without-brokerage
App: https://getfoliospan.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=free2026

articles.author: Dat Dtek
articles.description:
How I turn still wedding photos into a cinematic AI film (with prompts that actually work)


I make wedding films from still photos. No camera crew, no reshoot day — a couple sends me their photos, and I build a 60-second film they play at the reception.
The first ones I made were bad in a specific way. A photo plus a one-line prompt — "make this photo move, cinematic wedding video" — usually comes back with a warped face, flickering light, or hands that bend wrong. The model isn't being lazy. It is guessing, and a vague prompt gives it too much to guess about.
What fixed it for me was writing prompts like a shot list, not like a wish. One motion per clip. One model picked for one job. A storyboard with exact timings before I generate anything. I open-sourced the kit I built for myself — 3…

Your AI-built app probably leaks secrets. I wrote a CLI that checks before you launch


I keep seeing the same thing in AI-built apps. Someone vibes an app into existence over a weekend. It works, it looks good, and then they launch it with the database password sitting in a config file. Nobody checked.
I wrote a small CLI that checks. It's called vibe-code-rescue, and it reads your code and writes a plain-language report with a grade. I built it because I kept finding the same mistakes in AI-built apps, including my own, and I wanted the checker I wished existed.
The fastest way to see what it does is the demo. The repo ships with a deliberately vulnerable app, and the audit takes ten seconds:
